data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a pragmatic, non-inductive decision rule based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness) rather than probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If corroboration is used to predict future success with any degree of confidence beyond 'it is the best bet we have', it smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference implies that the theory is more likely to be true than a falsified one, it violates the prohibition on probabilistic confirmation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical probability of a theory (which decreases with content) and its corroboration (a report on past performance). The mechanism is a 'critical preference': we prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe tests because it has the highest potential verisimilitude among available options. This is not an inductive inference that the theory is true or probable, but a rational choice to act on the best-tested hypothesis while acknowledging it may be false tomorrow. It treats corroboration as a guide to action, not a measure of truth.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
